editorial.headline: The Kitchenware Wholesale Code That Stops at Bali’s PMA Gate
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 46491 embraces a broad household-goods wholesale trade nationally, yet Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium blocks its PMA registration.
editorial.body:
KBLI 46491 is a wholesale-trade classification for the practical objects that shape a kitchen and everyday household use. Its stated scope includes cookware such as pots and pans, as well as kitchen equipment. It also reaches consumer electronics—electric toothbrushes, radios, televisions, CD and DVD recorders and players, and stereo equipment. The range continues through porcelain and glass tableware, cutlery including spoons, knives and forks, wooden articles, woven goods and cork goods. What binds these varied products together is wholesale trade: the code gives a distributor a single classification for a deliberately broad basket of domestic and household-facing goods.

The activity is open at every listed scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That makes the classification relevant to wholesalers whose product range may run from kitchen and dining goods to consumer electronics and natural-material household articles. The breadth of the merchandise should not obscure the central point of the record, however. This is one defined wholesale activity, and its foreign-investment position has to be read in both the national and Bali settings.

Nationally, its PMA status is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership level of 100%. In plain terms, the national record allows full foreign ownership for this activity. That is the national ceiling, but it is not the final word for a company considering Bali. National openness does not override Bali’s block on PMA registration.

For a foreigner seeking PMA registration, the operative Bali answer is direct: this activity cannot be registered in Bali today. The Bali record identifies the issue as class-risk blocking. At the Besar scale, OSS risk is recorded as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope, bringing the activity within Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. The recorded trigger dates to May 2026. This is not a lower Bali foreign-ownership ceiling; it is a registration block for PMA in Bali, despite the national 100% position.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness does not override Bali’s block on PMA registration.
